explanations.explanation: Psalm 9:3 says, "When my enemies retreat, they stumble and perish before You." Retreating doesn't get them out of it. They run, and they still end up on the ground. That's a LOT of cardio for nothing, friend.
That's what a coach would draw up at halftime, but this verse has no second round. It says they "stumble and perish before You." The retreat doesn't turn into a comeback.

explanations.answer: They hide out in the hills
explanations.explanation: Hills are great for a picnic, friend, but the verse never sends them to any. It says, "they stumble and perish before You." They don't get away to a hiding spot, and the psalm doesn't mention one.

explanations.answer: As a judge on His throne judging righteously
explanations.explanation: Psalm 9:4 says, "You sit on Your throne judging righteously." A judge sits, listens and decides what's right, and here the LORD has upheld David's just cause. That's a steady picture, baker. Nobody has to wonder who's in charge of the room.

explanations.answer: As a soldier at the front leading the charge
explanations.explanation: I like the energy, but the verse doesn't put Him on a battlefield. It says He sits on His throne. A throne is a seat, and I've never seen a soldier charge in carrying a chair.

explanations.answer: As a shepherd in the field guarding the flock
explanations.explanation: The shepherd picture is real in Scripture, and David uses it for the LORD in Psalm 23:1. It's just not the picture in this verse. Here the LORD sits on His throne "judging righteously."
Psalm 9:5 says, "You have erased their name forever and ever." Forever and ever, baker. That's not pencil, and it's not even pencil with a cheap eraser.
Careful, the verse says just the opposite. Psalm 9:5 says, "You have erased their name forever and ever." It's not for a season or until next week, friend. It says forever and ever.
Close, but it's the other way around. Psalm 9:7 says, "But the LORD abides forever; He has established His throne for judgment." The enemy is gone, and the LORD stays. He's not going anywhere, baker.
Right, friend. The enemy is gone, but Psalm 9:7 says, "But the LORD abides forever." He also "has established His throne for judgment." No fading, no expiration date.
Psalm 9:9 says, "The LORD is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble." Both of those are places you run INTO. When trouble shows up, the oppressed know where to go, baker.

Those are warm words, but they aren't the ones David uses here. Psalm 9:9 calls the LORD "a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble." Think of a place to run to, friend, not a person to follow.

Those are jobs people do, and that's not what the verse is picturing. Psalm 9:9 says the LORD is "a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble." A refuge and a stronghold are places you can be safe in.
Psalm 9:10 says, "for You, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek You." The verse also says that those who know His name trust in Him. Seek Him, baker, and you're not talking to an empty room.
It's the other direction, friend. Psalm 9:10 says, "for You, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek You." Nobody who seeks Him gets left behind.
Psalm 9:12 says, "He does not ignore the cry of the afflicted." When the afflicted cry out, He doesn't look past them. Not once, baker.
Try it in the sentence, friend. "He does not hear the cry" would make Him deaf to it, and that's not what the verse says. Psalm 9:12 says He "does not ignore the cry of the afflicted."
Good word, but it doesn't fit the line. "He does not answer the cry" would say the opposite of what David means. Psalm 9:12 says the LORD "does not ignore the cry of the afflicted."

Psalm 9:14 gives the plan: "that I may declare all Your praises." Then he wants to rejoice in God's salvation "within the gates of Daughter Zion." The first thing on his list once he's lifted up is praise, baker.

explanations.answer: Take revenge on all his enemies
explanations.explanation: That's a natural guess, but the verse never says it. Psalm 9:14 says he wants to "declare all Your praises" and rejoice in God's salvation. His wish after being lifted up is to praise.

explanations.answer: Rest far away from his troubles
explanations.explanation: A quiet getaway sounds nice, friend, but that's not his plan. He wants to be where the people are, saying that "within the gates of Daughter Zion I may rejoice in Your salvation." (Psalm 9:14) He's going to the gates, not away from them.

Psalm 9:15 says, "The nations have fallen into a pit of their making; their feet are caught in the net they have hidden." They dug it and they hid it, then they landed in it. That's the oldest trap in the book, baker, and it's on the people who set it.
The verse doesn't catch David or his army. It says "The nations have fallen into a pit of their making." The trap they set is the trap they're stuck in.
Not them, friend. Psalm 9:15 says the nations "have fallen into a pit of their making." The net is the one "they have hidden," so it's on their own feet.

Half of it is right, because Psalm 9:17 says the wicked "will return to Sheol" with all the nations who forget God. But the second half flips the verse. Psalm 9:18 says, "For the needy will not always be forgotten."

You caught it, baker. The nations who forget God are headed for Sheol (Psalm 9:17), but the needy aren't forgotten forever. Psalm 9:18 says, "For the needy will not always be forgotten; nor the hope of the oppressed forever dashed."
Psalm 9:20 says, "let the nations know they are but men." It's a humbling reminder, baker. Big armies and big cities, and still just men in front of the LORD.
Zion is in the psalm, but not like that. Psalm 9:20 asks the LORD to "let the nations know they are but men." It says nothing about Zion ruling anybody.
David is the one writing the psalm, but he doesn't ask for that. What he asks is, "let the nations know they are but men." (Psalm 9:20) The point isn't who rules them, friend, it's what they are.
Psalm 10:2 says, "In pride the wicked pursue the needy." They go after the people with the least to defend themselves. That's why the psalmist is crying out, baker.
Priests aren't in this verse, friend. Psalm 10:2 says the wicked pursue "the needy." That's who is being chased.
The psalm doesn't mention kings here. It says, "In pride the wicked pursue the needy." The ones getting chased are the ones with the least, baker.
Psalm 10:4 says, "in all his schemes there is no God." Not one scheme with God in it, baker. Pride filled up the whole space.
That would at least be a phone call to God, and the verse doesn't give him one. It says, "in all his schemes there is no God." (Psalm 10:4) He doesn't make room even when things go badly for him.
The verse doesn't leave any special day. It says that in his pride the wicked man "does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God." (Psalm 10:4) No holy day, no exception.
Look at the second half, friend. Psalm 10:5 says, "Your lofty judgments are far from him." God's judgments are far from him, not close.
Right, baker. The first half is true, but Psalm 10:5 says, "Your lofty judgments are far from him." They're far from him, not close.
Psalm 10:9 says, "He lies in wait like a lion in a thicket; he lurks to seize the oppressed." A lion sits still in the brush and waits to pounce, baker. That's the picture.
A bear would be scary, but the psalmist picks a different animal. Psalm 10:9 says, "like a lion in a thicket." Same lurking, friend, different creature.
Wolves are in plenty of stories, but not this verse. Psalm 10:9 says the wicked man "lies in wait like a lion in a thicket." The hiding spot is a thicket, not a field.

explanations.answer: God has forgotten and never sees
explanations.explanation: Psalm 10:11 says, "He says to himself, 'God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees.'" That's what the wicked man tells himself, baker. It's his claim about God, and I'm glad the psalm doesn't leave it standing alone.
The wicked man isn't even thinking about forgiveness, friend. In Psalm 10:11 he says, "God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees." In his own mind, nobody is watching.

explanations.answer: God is fighting on his side
explanations.explanation: He doesn't claim that. Psalm 10:11 has him saying, "God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees." In his words, God isn't on any side because God isn't looking, baker.
It's the other way around, friend. Psalm 10:13 says the wicked man tells himself, "You will never call me to account." He's sure God won't make him answer for anything.
You've got it, baker. Psalm 10:13 has him saying to himself, "You will never call me to account." He's sure no reckoning is coming, and that's what the psalmist is arguing against.
Psalm 10:14 says, "The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless." The ones with nobody to stand up for them have Him, baker. It's a good thing to have in your corner.
The powerful already have plenty of help, friend. The verse says, "You are the helper of the fatherless." (Psalm 10:14) The LORD is the one standing with the victim.
Nice try, baker, but money isn't in this line. Psalm 10:14 says, "You are the helper of the fatherless." It's about the one with no father to stand up for them.

Psalm 10:15 says, "Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call him to account for his wickedness until none is left to be found." The arm is what he used against the helpless. The psalmist is asking God to deal with it, baker.
A bow is a decent guess, but it's not the word in the verse. Psalm 10:15 says, "Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer." It's his arm, friend, not his gear.
No walls get broken in this verse. The psalmist asks, "Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer." (Psalm 10:15) The request is about the wicked man himself, baker.
Psalm 10:17 says, "You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their hearts." The humble get heard and strengthened. That's a good deal for anybody, baker.
The proud are the ones in the wicked man's corner of this psalm, friend. Psalm 10:17 says, "You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble." The LORD hears and strengthens the humble.
The mighty have their own strength already. The verse says, "You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their hearts." (Psalm 10:17) It's the humble who get heard, baker.

That's what the psalm says, baker. Psalm 10:17 says, "You will incline Your ear," and verse 18 goes on, "to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, that the men of the earth may strike terror no more." It's a good place for the psalm to land, with God leaning in to listen.

That's actually what the psalm says, friend. Psalm 10:17 says, "You will incline Your ear," and verse 18 continues, "to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, that the men of the earth may strike terror no more." The psalm ends with God listening and the terror stopping.
